Book collections, deliver authorized reports and escalate critical values

Labs and imaging centers handle a high volume of short interactions: price enquiries, home collection slots, report requests and doctor calls. We automate the routine work around your LIS, while report authorization, critical value calls and result interpretation stay with pathologists and radiologists.

What makes diagnostics & pathology labs different

  • Home collection requests arrive by phone and chat, and phlebotomist routes are planned by hand each morning.

  • Patients and referring doctors call repeatedly to ask whether a report is ready.

  • Critical values depend on someone noticing a flag at night and finding the right clinician, with inconsistent records of the call.

  • Referring doctor relationships are managed from memory, with little visibility of turnaround complaints or failed report deliveries.

Where automation helps diagnostics & pathology labs

  • Test and package enquiries

    Prices, preparation and collection timings answered from the lab's approved test master; clinical questions go to the lab's medical staff.

  • Home collection scheduling

    Pincode serviceability, slot booking, phlebotomist assignment and arrival updates, with each test list confirmed against the prescription by a coordinator.

  • Report-ready notifications

    Secure, expiring report links sent only after authorization in the LIS or RIS, with copies to referring doctors where the patient has agreed.

  • Critical value escalation

    LIS critical flags page the on-duty pathologist, who phones the clinician and records the read-back, with an escalation ladder for unacknowledged alerts.

  • Referring doctor service desk

    A CRM view of each referring doctor's report preferences, turnaround issues and open tickets, built without any referral incentive fields.

  • Turnaround complaints and recovery

    Feedback after report delivery, with delays and report errors routed to the lab quality manager for call-back and root-cause review.

Find and enquireStandard3–4 weeks

Safe enquiry routing for clinics and labs

Incoming WhatsApp and website messages are sorted by intent. Fees, timings, check-up packages, test preparation and directions are answered from approved content; symptoms, result questions and complaints go to the right staff member, and emergencies get an immediate instruction.

Clinics & day-care centres · Diagnostics & pathology labs

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Small teams cannot answer every message quickly, and generic chatbots either frustrate patients or, worse, attempt medical advice. Enquiries left unanswered often book elsewhere, while messages that describe symptoms need a qualified person, not a template.

Trigger

A patient sends a WhatsApp message to the clinic or lab number, or submits the website enquiry form.

How it runs

  1. Open a conversation linked to the CRM contact, creating it if new; replies inside the 24-hour service window need no template, and later follow-ups use approved templates only for patients who opted in.
  2. Screen each message first against the emergency word list agreed with the clinical lead; on a match, reply at once with the facility's emergency number and 112 and alert the duty staff.
  3. Classify the remaining text into intents such as fees, timings, check-up packages, test preparation, booking, report status, symptom or complaint, with a confidence score.
  4. Answer administrative intents only from the approved FAQ, rate card or test master, citing the entry used; low-confidence drafts are not sent.
  5. Hand symptom, medicine and result questions to the nurse or lab medical staff queue with a conversation summary, and tell the patient who will reply and when.
  6. Log intent, handoff reason and response times for a weekly review of wording and routing rules.

Human checkpoint

The clinic nurse or the lab's medical officer answers every symptom, medicine or result question; front-office staff take complaints and anything the model is unsure about. The clinical lead approves the emergency word list and the FAQ before go-live.

Message bodies are deleted after the facility's retention period. Model calls run under enterprise terms without training on the data, and staff access is role-based.

Book and prepareStandard4–6 weeks

Home sample collection scheduling and phlebotomist routing

Collection requests from WhatsApp, the website or the call center are checked for serviceable pincodes, booked into slots, batched into phlebotomist routes and tracked through to barcode handover at the lab.

Diagnostics & pathology labs

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Collection bookings arrive through several channels and coordinators plan routes by hand each morning. Patients are unsure when the phlebotomist will arrive or whether they should fast, and late or missed visits lead to repeat collections and unhappy referring doctors.

Trigger

A patient requests a home collection, or a referring doctor's order marked for home collection is entered in the LIS.

How it runs

  1. Capture address, pincode, preferred window and test list through a WhatsApp Flow or web form, with any prescription image uploaded through a secure link rather than as a chat attachment.
  2. Check serviceability and slot capacity, hold the slot and confirm with fasting and preparation notes from the lab's test master.
  3. Queue the request for a coordinator to confirm the test list against the prescription before the visit.
  4. Batch confirmed visits into routes by area and assign phlebotomists in the scheduling board.
  5. Send day-of updates with the phlebotomist's name and arrival window; a delay triggers a revised window and a coordinator alert.
  6. Record barcode scans at collection and at lab receipt, and flag samples that miss the transport window set by the lab.

Human checkpoint

The collection coordinator confirms every test list against the prescription and resolves special preparation questions with the lab's medical officer. The phlebotomist verifies the patient's identity on site before collecting.

Results and reportsStandard4–6 weeks

Consented lab and radiology report delivery

Once a pathologist or radiologist authorizes a report, the patient receives a notification with a secure, expiring link, and the referring doctor gets a copy only where the patient agreed. Reports are linked to ABHA where the lab participates in ABDM.

Diagnostics & pathology labs

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Patients call to ask whether reports are ready, staff forward PDFs from personal phones, and nobody can show who received a report. Forwarded attachments also carry health data into chats the lab cannot control.

Trigger

A report's status changes to authorized in the LIS or RIS.

How it runs

  1. Check the patient's delivery preference and consent for patient and referring-doctor copies.
  2. Send an approved template saying the report is ready, with a secure link that asks for a one-time code sent to the registered mobile number before opening.
  3. Send one reminder if the link is not opened within the lab's chosen window, and offer collection or email as alternatives.
  4. Deliver the referring doctor's copy to their preferred channel where the patient has agreed.
  5. Where the lab is ABDM-integrated, trigger the LIS to link the report to the patient's ABHA for consented sharing.
  6. Log every delivery, open and failure for audit and for the lab's turnaround reporting.

Human checkpoint

Only reports authorized by a pathologist or radiologist are released, and the automation never explains results. Questions about a result go to the lab's medical staff or the referring doctor, and critical values follow the escalation path before any notification.

Results and reportsStandard3–5 weeks

Critical result escalation with recorded read-back

When the LIS flags a result outside the lab's approved critical limits, the on-duty pathologist is paged at once, phones the responsible clinician and records the read-back. Unacknowledged alerts climb an agreed escalation ladder.

Diagnostics & pathology labs

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Critical values depend on someone noticing a flag and reaching the right clinician by phone, often at night. Calls are not always recorded consistently, while accreditation assessors expect a documented procedure and evidence of who was told and when.

Trigger

The LIS marks a result as critical against the lab's approved critical value list.

How it runs

  1. Open an escalation case with lab ID, test, value, sample time and the referring or treating clinician's contact details.
  2. Page the on-duty pathologist or senior technologist through the lab's internal channel and a DLT-registered SMS template.
  3. The pathologist verifies the result and phones the clinician, or the patient where there is no referring clinician, then records who received it, the time and the read-back.
  4. If the case is not acknowledged within the window set in the lab's procedure, escalate to the backup pathologist and then the lab director.
  5. Report notification times and incomplete records each week to the quality manager.

Human checkpoint

A pathologist or senior technologist verifies every critical result and speaks personally to the clinician, or to the patient when there is no referring clinician. The automation never puts critical values in messages or interprets them; it pages people and keeps the record.

Feedback and relationshipsStarter3–4 weeks

Referring-doctor relationship CRM

Each referring doctor and clinic gets a CRM record of report preferences, turnaround issues, open tickets and service reviews, so relationship managers fix problems early. The CRM has no fields for referral payments, which medical ethics rules prohibit.

Diagnostics & pathology labs

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Labs depend on doctors who refer patients and samples, yet relationship managers work from memory and call logs. Turnaround complaints and delivery failures surface late, and informal arrangements can drift towards referral incentives that the NMC ethics regulations prohibit for doctors.

Trigger

A new referring doctor appears in LIS orders, a doctor raises an issue, or a monthly service review is due.

How it runs

  1. Create or update the doctor's CRM record from LIS referral fields, with the registration number checked against the medical council register or Healthcare Professionals Registry, and the preferred report channel.
  2. Log turnaround delays, report errors and delivery failures for that doctor's patients as linked issues with owners and due dates.
  3. Alert the relationship manager when issues repeat for a doctor or pass their due date.
  4. Prepare a monthly service summary per doctor with aggregated volumes and open issues for the relationship manager.
  5. Leave out any field or workflow for commissions, gifts or fee sharing in the CRM configuration.

Human checkpoint

The relationship manager owns each doctor record and decides on follow-up, and the lab director reviews the monthly summaries. Commercial terms with hospitals and institutions are handled by management outside the automation, under the lab's ethics policy.

Feedback and relationshipsStarter2–4 weeks

Patient feedback and service recovery

A short feedback request follows each visit, discharge, report or pharmacy order. Low scores and complaints open tickets with owners and deadlines, possible clinical concerns go to the quality team, and themes are reviewed every week.

Multi-specialty hospitals · Diagnostics & pathology labs · Pharmacies & medical retail

Open the automation blueprint

The problem

Feedback is collected on paper or not at all, complaints surface first in public reviews, and nobody tracks whether an unhappy patient was called back. Clinical concerns hidden in feedback comments can go unseen.

Trigger

A visit is closed, a patient is discharged, a report is delivered or a pharmacy order is completed.

How it runs

  1. Send one feedback request per episode, with a rating and optional comment, on the channel the patient opted into: WhatsApp for hospitals and labs, SMS or email for pharmacy orders.
  2. Classify comments by theme, such as waiting, billing, staff behavior, cleanliness or possible clinical concern, using a model whose labels staff review.
  3. Open a service recovery ticket for low ratings and complaints, assigned to the patient relations or store manager with a call-back deadline.
  4. Send possible clinical concerns to the quality manager or medical superintendent under the facility's grievance procedure.
  5. Close tickets only with a recorded outcome, and send weekly theme and closure reports to department heads.

Human checkpoint

Patient relations staff or the store manager call every low-score patient, and the quality team or medical superintendent reviews any comment that may describe a clinical problem. Model theme labels are checked during the weekly review.
